💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the tech giant mentioned.
  • The startup came out of stealth in August.
  • Recent findings suggest that corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense.

Recent findings suggest that three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the tech giant mentioned. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

The startup came out of stealth in August. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Another flaw was found in Node.js, the open source JavaScript runtime environment. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. The day showcased the kind of onslaught on security that AI has enabled.

Recent findings suggest that corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

NASA Science Data Powers Upcoming Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.
  • Recent findings suggest that an international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before.
  • Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.

Recent findings suggest that an international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.

Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.

By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.

A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.

"We don't see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can't just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from," said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”.

Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.

Recent findings suggest that gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers. The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.

"We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data," Gazith said.

Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.

The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.

"We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn't find," stated Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. "The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the upcoming algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”.

The discovery would not have happened without NASA's longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.

"The nice thing about NASA data is it's all open," Clark said. "All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.".

Recent findings suggest that that openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely upcoming approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA's Fermitools, enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.

The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with latest findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.

Sources indicate that "Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search," remarked Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "It's made all of the science better.".

Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

Sources indicate that that’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a latest tech giant with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

Recent findings suggest that the startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

Recent findings suggest that “When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

Sources indicate that “Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan mentioned. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

Industry observers note that “It was really crucial that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.

It has been revealed that internet connection speeds are consistently rising most everywhere in the world, and more than a few spots already have multi-gigabit service available. Making those kinds of speeds available throughout your house, however, requires a competent router that can handle both the high throughput and a fairly high number of connected devices. Enter the TP-Link Archer BE9500 Wi-Fi 7 router with 10 Gbps WAN, which, as of right now, is on sale at Best Buy for under a single Benjamin, at $89.99 — or under half its regular price of $199.99.

Industry observers note that TP-Link networking gear has earned a good reputation with techies thanks to good reliability and offering great specs at quite affordable pricing, as is the case in point. Unlike some routers that outright lie about supporting WiFi 7, the Archer BE9500 actually has the magical combo that fully enables the power of the latest protocol: a 6 GHz band, along with Multi Link Operation (MLO) support.

The TP-Link Archer BE9500 is a full-featured Wi-Fi 7 router with full 6 GHz and MLO support and a 10 Gbps WAN port for high-speed internet connections.

It has been revealed that that grants the BE9500 an entire 9.5 Gbps of combined wireless bandwidth across all three frequencies, broadcast into the airwaves by six beam-forming antennas. For physical connections, there's one 10 Gbps WAN port, along with two 2.5 Gbps connectors for your substantial workstations or gaming rigs, and an additional two gigabit ports.

Sources indicate that as befits a modern router, the Archer BE9500 supports EasyMesh for wiring additional devices, as well as separate guest and internal networks for segregating IoT and other classes of devices. There are four VPN flavors on offer for acting as both a server and a client, including support for the modern WireGuard protocol.

A USB port for connecting storage media, parental controls, automatic firmware upgrade, VLAN tagging, and miscellaneous features round out the main features. Get this router while stocks last, for only $89.99 at Best Buy.

From AAA hits to indie darlings, Epic has really made its mark with free games. You can even snag these games if you don't have a powerful PC so you can play them if you ever get one. Look at the list below to see the frankly ridiculous list of free games that have been available. Industry News: Have you ever been told that there was something about you that was ‘too much’?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And right now, I’m at two inflection points: approaching 10 years of being in business and the end of another calendar year.
  • And right now, I’m at two inflection points: approaching 10 years of being in business and the end of another calendar year.
  • It has been revealed that for example, I am indecisive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inflection points spark reflection. And right now, I’m at two inflection points: approaching 10 years of being in business and the end of another calendar year. One of the things I am recalling is that as a woman, some of my characteristics that I once thought of as deficits have conspired to be my greatest assets. Unbeknownst to me, they are actually the factors that contribute to my success. For example, I am indecisive. I constantly weigh the pros and cons of a situation. I blame that in part on being a Libra — but that trait is also why I loved studying cultural anthropology and gravitate towards multidisciplinary work. In my job history I was sometimes told that I had to “pick a lane.. And it’s been brought to my attention multiple times, especially in corporate environments, that decisiveness is a winning attribute. But as I have evolved, my indecisiveness is the very quality that helps me consider multiple perspectives and identify alternative future scenarios of a situation. Ironically, my indecisiveness helps me navigate ambiguous terrain. How wonderful that years later that ability to straddle lanes and work in multidisciplinary environments has become my asset as I’ve built a manufacturer to help people toggle between wonder and rigor. What about others? I was curious to learn from other women if an inherent quality that they were told was “too much” turned out to be a creative asset in their work. Bear with me — I know that such a question could be posed to men too. But in my experience, it’s women who tend to contort themselves in order to fit into the workplace. This phenomenon is called “covering.” According to a 2024 Deloitte report in collaboration with the NYU Meltzer Center, covering is when people feel the need to downplay certain identities in order to fit in at work. The report found that cisgender women are more likely to cover than are cisgender men. So for the purposes of this exploration I am focusing on women. Sheila Lirio Marcelo, the founder and CEO of Ohai and founder of Care.com shared a time when two mentors took her to lunch to tell her that she was “too intense.. She was able to take the feedback and reflected in the following way: “They were right. I cared enormously about the work, but I hadn’t yet learned to separate my intensity about the outcome from how I showed up with people. That conversation changed how I lead. I developed a mantra: Be intense about outcomes, but chill with people.” First, what maturity in Sheila’s ability to take that feedback! Second, what a great reframe on her part. She never disavowed herself of her innate intensity. Instead she converted that intensity into a creative asset. As Sheila put it, that intensity was “the drive to question what others accept, imagine a different answer, and keep pushing until we build it- while giving people the space and trust to get there.” Daisy Auger Dominguez, Chief People Officer at Digital Asset shared a similar story: “I’ve been told that I bring too much passion and joy to work, as though enthusiasm somehow diminishes seriousness or credibility. “Early in my career, I sometimes felt pressure to temper both to be taken seriously. But I’ve learned that joy and rigor aren’t mutually exclusive. My passion fuels my curiosity and creativity, and joy creates the conditions for others to imagine, contribute, and take risks alongside me. Some of my most meaningful work has come from bringing people together around possibilities they couldn’t yet see. What was once considered “too much” became how I bring others along.” The lesson There’s a lesson here for all of us who manage women. I call it inside-out leadership: the ability to be more transparent, humble and curious about the inner lives of those we lead and of ourselves. Consider the following questions: Are there qualities in some of the women on your team that are innate personality traits that could be assets, as in the case of Daisy Auger Dominguez? How might you draw that out in them? Is it worth having a constructive conversation, as in the case of Sheila Lirio, so that you help the woman reframe it as an asset? Are you, as a manager, covering? Could that be to your and your team’s detriment? Or, are you transparent about your unique qualities and encourage your teammates to heighten theirs for the betterment of the work? These questions are a starting point to ensure that women thrive, that work flourishes, and that in a time when AI can do basic tasks, we add texture to our work by leaning into what makes us uniquely human.

SEO Isn’t Over, But Google Is Losing Its Monopoly. Here’s How to Adapt.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Like clockwork, the digital marketing echo chamber sounds the death knell every few years: “SEO is dead.”.
  • In a recent development, I entered this game in the early 2000s as a web developer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Like clockwork, the digital marketing echo chamber sounds the death knell every few years: “SEO is dead.”.

In a recent development, I entered this game in the early 2000s as a web developer. I was building sites at night while working a full-time job during the day. If I wanted traffic, I had to figure out search engine optimization through trial and error.

My first transactional store lived on Yahoo! Stores, selling generic mini MP3 players — that is, until the iPod wiped that category out overnight. Next, I sold GPS navigation software on CDs, which stopped when the iPhone made standalone navigation devices obsolete.

Then came an ecommerce brand called Soccer Nation. Growth happened fast. We opened a physical storefront in Vista, California, at the same time that David Beckham signed with the LA Galaxy of the MLS, and watched revenue climb for years. Then the 2008 recession froze retail spending. We shuttered the retail shop and sold the domain to a competitor who turned it into an online soccer publication.

This is important because I’ve spent more than two decades watching technological and economic disruptions dismantle business models. Every time Google rolled out a major algorithm revision — Panda, Penguin, Hummingbird, Helpful Content — the same panic ensued. Marketers declared that search was finished. I pushed back each time with: “SEO isn’t dead. It’s just evolving.”.

This time, however, the underlying shift is fundamentally different from anything we’ve seen over the past 25 years.

It has been revealed that in prior cycles, the rules changed, but the referee stayed the same. Google updated its algorithms, penalized black-hat tactics and forced brands to create better experiences. Through it all, Mountain View remained the undisputed gatekeeper of the internet.

Recent findings suggest that google isn’t just updating the rules this time. It is losing its monopoly over human intent.

According to recent reports, discovery is decentralizing. Consumers no longer instinctively open a browser window, navigate to a search bar and wade through ten blue links buried beneath four sponsored ads. Instead, discovery happens natively where people live, via ambient operating systems, vertical AI engines and conversational interfaces.

Take my own household as a real-world case study:.

I genuinely can’t remember anyone in my family running a standard Google search.

Industry observers note that this behavioral pivot is driving massive market shifts. Tech market corrections and capital reallocations, such as Alphabet shedding hundreds of billions in market cap during major competitive platform announcements, are not anomalies. They are a lagging indicator of a structural reality: Google’s absolute control over the web’s front door has permanently fractured.

As user behavior shifts from rigid keywords (“best running shoes flat feet”) to complex, conversational prompts (“Compare the top stability running shoes for wide, flat feet under $200 with solid arch support for marathon prep”), standard keyword density and thin programmatic landing pages fail completely.

Enter Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), also referred to as Generative Engine Optimization (GEO).

If your marketing leadership is still treating AEO as a minor technical checklist item — uploading an llms.txt file, structuring basic JSON-LD schema and tweaking H2s to question formats — you are missing the forest for the trees.

Winning citation share inside modern language models demands an integrated on-page and off-page architecture built around four core pillars:.

Large language models prioritize information efficiency. Models bypass content that regurgitates commodity definitions. Winning content provides primary data, original research, proprietary case studies and clear, structured answers that an engine can cleanly ingest and quote without wading through filler.

LLMs operate on probabilistic associative networks and massive training corpora. If authoritative industry publications, trade journals and top-tier editorial outlets do not regularly cite your brand in direct association with your specific vertical, the model won’t know you exist. Instead, it will synthesize and recommend your competitors.

Answer engines heavily weigh verified public consensus. Unstructured discussions across Reddit, niche communities, review aggregators and professional directories serve as foundational data for conversational engines. Unmonitored reputation issues or a total absence from peer-to-peer discourse directly leads to exclusion from AI recommendations.

In a recent development, AEO requires managing how your brand is perceived across multiple distinct engines, such as Perplexity, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Meta AI. Because these systems ingest public social platforms to gauge real-time cultural relevance and expertise, your organic social footprint and executive thought leadership now directly fuel your search visibility.

SEO is not dead, but gone are the days of optimizing exclusively for a single search engine algorithm.

According to recent reports, sustainable organic visibility requires understanding how multi-modal models ingest, evaluate, synthesize and attribute authoritative sources across the entire open web. For entrepreneurs and executives planning growth initiatives, ensuring your business is cited, trusted and surfaced by generative answer engines is no longer an experimental line item. It is foundational to enterprise value.

Find out if AI search engines cite your content. Get your AEO and GEO readiness score for free to see how your website stacks up across four core visibility factors.

Like clockwork, the digital marketing echo chamber sounds the death knell every few years: “SEO is dead.”.

Sources indicate that I entered this game in the early 2000s as a web developer. I was building sites at night while working a full-time job during the day. If I wanted traffic, I had to figure out search engine optimization through trial and error.

My first transactional store lived on Yahoo! Stores, selling generic mini MP3 players — that is, until the iPod wiped that category out overnight. Next, I sold GPS navigation software on CDs, which stopped when the iPhone made standalone navigation devices obsolete.

Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.
  • Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.
  • With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass latest protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block consumers from filing lawsuits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.

Congress is scrambling to provide legal recourse for deepfakes and online grooming.

With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass latest protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block consumers from filing lawsuits.

It has been revealed that on Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against people who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.

According to recent reports, “The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a upcoming bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.

“The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”.

Roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that users were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the tech giant’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”.

According to recent reports, roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place owners under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a firm’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

Industry observers note that congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a fresh Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.

Litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake problem through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a newly introduced wave of legal challenges.

“You will be amazed by how rapidly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”.

According to recent reports, in addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how promptly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”.

The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she mentioned she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”.

Hilton stated over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”.

Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who stated a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how rapidly technology advances.”.

Recent findings suggest that needless to say, there are lots of people out there currently playing Grand Theft Auto 6, and despite what a lot of headlines and social media jokes insist, itâs not solely a boysâ club. Obviously, both my partner and I are game journalists, and both of us have worked in this industry for many years. When we first started living together, after she moved to San Francisco to join IGN, I foresaw a situation in which we would both have to review games at the same time. Maybe, then, it would make sense for us to have setups that allowed us to play different consoles simultaneously, maybe in different rooms or parts of the same room.

âWhy not just put them next to each other?â she posited as we mentally planned out our apartment. Why not, indeed!

That birthed what visiting friends all point out is a truly odd setup, but one that occasionally pays dividends. In the setup, we have my TV on the left and her TV on the right. The consoles on the left side are mine and only hook into my TV, while the consoles on the right side do the same to her TV, with the PC in the middle duplicating the image to both. Usually one person will wear headphones if weâre both playing something.

This works out well with a lot of games. When Tears of the Kingdom introduced at midnight, an informal race to get all the shrines motivated us to solve puzzles in more interesting ways than the other person.

With Grand Theft Auto 6, though, it allowed us to see exactly what little details were changing in the game depending on our different actions and approaches.

In the gameâs prologue, Lucia tries her best to make it back to a coffee shop while the police search for her, scouring the city block. Since itâs mere minutes after the opening of the game, my partner and I got there at roughly the same time. She, pragmatic as she is, chose to walk along the sidewalks until the cops eventually picked her up. I tried to cut around the building and swim, and then I got hit in the head by a police boat and was knocked unconscious. Whoops.

For me, in the cutscene that followed, Lucia was being handcuffed to a gurney while EMS and police pushed her into the back of an ambulance. For my partner, Lucia was being manhandled by police into the back of a cop car. In both situations, she pleaded about needing to go back to the coffee shop, but it was maybe a bit more fraught and scary in my case as she fought to maintain consciousness.Â.

Recent findings suggest that the scenes were similar, but different, and it was fascinating to be able to watch them side-by-side like this. That wow factor has kind of kept up throughout as we’ve continued playing. In an early mission, I watched her, playing as Jason, enter a car impound lot in a completely different way than I had. She gave me tips about when I would be able to play as Lucia, noticing that I was bumming around a lot (to which I answered, âBut I have to make sure sheâs happy with the house first.â)Â.

I wonder if Iâm signing up for a lifetime of doing more chores without realizing it.

Or maybe three screens is the perfect number?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for U.S. President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers—China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin—was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America’s toughest rivals. Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. They were to discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran and how to reduce the dangers posed by nuclear arsenals. But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels, and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court. What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump swiftly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin. Still, he hailed the visit as “highly consequential” on social media as he made his way back to Washington and announced he would hold a press conference on Friday at the White House. The agreements stemming from the trilateral meeting were modest, but the rhetoric that came at the start of it was not. “We are really making history,” Trump said. “The United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used.” Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on “promoting world peace.” Putin, for his part, said the countries “hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace.” After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive, and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format “useful and substantive.” “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said in response to a question about whether the image of the meeting itself mattered more than the substance. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved, and modernized” deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals. “We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin, and Trump,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.” The leaders also talked about Iran and trade The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year. Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America. Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade complications. Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine. “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said, calling Putin “my friend.” Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war. After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel. Trump boasts about his relationships, but the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger The U.S. president’s ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine—or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan, and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks. Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug. But for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, he did not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share. On Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed new sanctions. By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December. There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi. Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session. And Chinese television showed a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator. —By Josh Boak, Michelle L. It has been revealed that xi noted that relations between the U.S. and China have been “generally stable and improved” during Trump’s presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade problems.

Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia’s war in Ukraine.

“Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump noted, calling Putin “my friend.”.

In a recent development, trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected fresh Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump’s administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

The U.S. president’s ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine—or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan, and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi made a symbolic gesture of friendship Wednesday by taking the unusual step of greeting Air Force One on the tarmac, and the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

According to recent reports, but for all the compliments the U.S. president has showered on the two autocrats, he did not always appear to have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share.

Sources indicate that on Wednesday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend.” The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend.” China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the U.S. and its allies imposed upcoming sanctions.

By contrast, when Xi went to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Trump and Xi have one more meeting planned this year, at the G20 summit in Florida in December.

There were also signs of friction Thursday in the U.S.-China relationship despite Trump’s praise of Xi.

Chinese officials blocked a Bloomberg reporter from the trilateral meeting after she asked a question at the earlier Trump-Xi session. And Chinese television demonstrated a video of Trump appearing drowsy, while the White House posted a clip of Trump helping Xi up an escalator.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It looks comparatively cheap — and that might be a good thing in this economy.

It looks comparatively cheap — and that might be a good thing in this economy.

In a recent development, for a while there, it seemed like Lenovo had given up on selling handheld gaming PCs, hiking the price of its Legion Go 2 and Legion Go S far higher than other RAM-starved competitors. A decent one can easily cost $1,000 if not $2,000 now. But it looks like Lenovo might be about to announce a relatively cheap handheld once again— the Legion Go Beam.

According to recent reports, windows Latest has leaked images of the handheld, and there’s no question it’s designed to be a value alternative to even the manufacturer’s least expensive Legion Go S variant. While it’s got the same major stippled grips and triggers for comfort, there’s only one USB-C port on the top instead of two, a comparatively cheap-looking D-pad, no touchpad, and only a single tiny intake and exhaust for its fan.

There’s no SteamOS logo where that would go, so it likely runs Windows instead… but then there’s that name, “Beam.” Perhaps you’ll “beam” your games to it because it’s a streaming and cloud gaming handheld, instead of one that primarily plays games on its own chip? Maybe that’s why it doesn’t need as much airflow as previous handhelds?

Perhaps there’s a partnership with Xbox Cloud Gaming specifically, and that’s why it’s all lit up in Xbox green?

Recent findings suggest that but it might just be green because it looks nice with white, which has been the “value” color for handhelds so far (see: ROG Ally, Xbox Ally, and the Windows-based Legion Go S). And it might be “Beam” because there’s a literal beam of light on the bottom, even though the first thing I do with most handhelds is turn any and all distracting RGB lighting off. Or maybe it’s “Beam” just because it sounds like a friendly, fun, value-oriented name, instead of something “S” or “Pro.”.

I won’t begin to speculate on the Legion Go Beam’s price, except to say that “cheap” may be relative. The Legion Go S was originally supposed to cost $499, but wound up costing far more except on the occasional sale. The Legion Go 2 was supposed to start at $1,099 but wound up costing $1,500 and up after RAMageddon. Streaming-first handhelds have been far cheaper, though, like the $249 Sony PlayStation Portal.

Lenovo has a history of announcing its new gaming devices at CES in January each year, including previous Legion Go handhelds, so I’m expecting to see an official announcement of the Lenovo Legion Go Beam then. Even if so, that doesn’t mean it’ll be available in January — there’s often a many-month lag.

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of famous faces and voices behind its many, many characters. From Bobby Moynihan as your verbose bestie to Weird Al Yankovic as a radio host, there's plenty of star power here--and you can even spot an influential figure from GTA history making a quick cameo. Spoilers below Who could it be now? In one of the later missions, players accompany Boobie on one of his errands. Once they reach a upcoming club, Boobie meets up with Big Mike and throws a few jibes at the local help sweeping the floor. That "little Santa" with the broom? None other than Rockstar Games president Sam Houser, who doesn't speak a single word in his brief appearance. As an added touch, Houser's digital doppelganger wears a white t-shirt with the Rockstar Games logo. Because the thumbnail for it is a big ol' spoiler, you can click this link to see the Houser cameo for yourself. This isn't the first time that Houser has cameoed in one of his studio's games. In GTA 3, he voiced one of the Ammu-Nation store clerks, and in GTA: San Andreas, a statue of that Ammu-Nation employee could be found in the game's Downtown Square area. Beyond minor background pedestrian and gangster voice roles in San Andreas and GTA 4, Houser has generally kept a low profile, focusing instead on developing the studio's games. With GTA 6 launching to major critical and commercial success, Houser has also issued a rare statement to mark the occasion. "This is a narrative set in a world of possibilities--and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels and concludes," he said. Meanwhile, Houser's brother, Dan Houser, is working on an open-world comedy game at Absurd Ventures, the studio he founded after leaving Rockstar Games in 2020. For more on GTA 6, check out GameSpot's Grand Theft Auto 6 guides hub for tips, tricks, and walkthroughs.

Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that investors in the latest round valued the tech giant at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the manufacturer said in a blog post.

Sources indicate that investors in the latest round valued the tech giant at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

According to recent reports, science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for newly introduced conditions.

Hodak revealed that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

With the funding, the firm aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s major ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The organization is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

#36. Measles is back, and it’s a dire warning against shrinking the U.S. government

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2953 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Measles is back, and it’s a dire warning against shrinking the U.S. government

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes, you really don’t know what you’ve got ’til it’s gone.
  • It has been revealed that sometimes, you really don’t know what you’ve got ’til it’s gone.
  • According to recent reports, unfortunately, this genre of realization stands to become a lot more common.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes, you really don’t know what you’ve got ’til it’s gone. Take, for instance, the United States’ measles elimination status. Formally rescinded this week, after a 26-year run, the Pan American Health Organization’s fresh determination is about to make a lot of people realize what a quiet miracle it was to never have to think about measles. Unfortunately, this genre of realization stands to become a lot more common. The official return of measles is just the starkest domestic example yet of the consequences that come with being led by an administration pot-committed to shrinking the federal government. The U.S. spent the last century building institutions that provided federal education programs, environmental regulations, consumer protections, and other services benefiting the public. Although these institutions didn’t always work perfectly, they generally either improved U.S. citizens’ lives or shielded them from harm that local governments weren’t equipped to manage on their own. And for at least the 45 years since Ronald Reagan famously declared government was not the solution to America’s problem, but rather the problem itself, tearing down these institutions has been a holy-grail goal for some conservatives. The most ardent proponents of that goal saw in Trump 2 a glimmering opportunity to dismantle the administrative state, as outlined extensively in the Project 2025 agenda. With the architect of Project 2025, Russell Vought, installed as White House budget director, the last two years have seen the steady evaporation or reorientation of institutions like the Department of Education, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), and of course, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), whose current incarnation helped usher in the measles resurgence. That result may be a preview of what happens when we lose mechanisms that solve certain problems so thoroughly that people seem to forget they were ever problems in the first place. It’s proof that weakening public protections doesn’t remove the need for those protections; it just makes us much less ready to combat everything they were protecting us from. How we got measles again Hours before news broke about America’s measles elimination status, current head of HHS Robert Kennedy Jr. used social media to respond to a different breaking news story. He posted on X an AI-generated image of himself mimicking the photo Amazon MGM used to promote Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. In the image, a tuxedo-clad Kennedy is holding an enormous carrot instead of 007’s gun, and the caption reads: “Food. Real food.” It would be hard to find a more apt representation of Kennedy’s tenure as the agency’s leader—a ridiculous, self-aggrandizing folly that depicts Kennedy as laser-focused on improving the quality of Americans’ food while actively ignoring the measles catastrophe he helped create. Food. Real Food. https://t.co/Tz0ePknCvg pic.twitter.com/tQPpeLbfH1— Secretary Kennedy (@SecKennedy) November 16, 2026 Vaccination rates had already been declining since the pandemic, when hesitancy and outright opposition spread virally through so-called wellness influencers and other bad actors. Instead of addressing this trend as the dire threat it was, Trump put in charge of HHS someone who has promoted anti-vaccine positions for decades. Within months, Kennedy was undermining the conventional wisdom around measles vaccinations in settings as public as the Dr. Phil TV show. Even more damaging: Kennedy kicked off his time at HHS by cutting $11 billion in state and local public-health grants. Those cuts forced health departments across the country to reduce staff, scale back critical services and, yes, either trim down or close various vaccination programs. Suddenly, the wastewater inspections, outbreak response teams, and buses traveling to areas riven by vaccine hesitancy were cut off at the knees. Amid Kennedy’s efforts to change the childhood vaccination schedule and dispute the number of measles cases and deaths, the U.S. has reported 5,412 confirmed cases through November 13—more than double the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. State health departments have also reported 10 measles-related deaths so far this year, up from three last year. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, cases have now surfaced in 46 states as well as Washington, D.C. This is exactly the sort of result HHS’s supposedly bloated budget existed to prevent. Shrinkage The same governing philosophy that helped set U.S. measles prevention back to the 1950s has also led to downsizing in several other institutions over the past two years—with even more devastating consequences in some cases. Shortly after Trump’s second inauguration last year, his White House functionally destroyed the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the primary department coordinating foreign development and humanitarian assistance around the globe. Before January 2025, USAID had approximately 13,600 employees; by April, only 241 remained. Annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion throughout the year, and the White House canceled roughly $80.5 billion in USAID and State Department foreign aid awards. Although Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a waiver for lifesaving humanitarian assistance programs, he added a laundry list of politically charged exemptions. These included programs involving abortions, family planning, “gender or DEI ideology programs,” and transgender surgeries. Because HIV/AIDS prevention didn’t fall under that waiver, and thanks to severe cuts to the George W. Bush-created President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), 1,700 HIV treatment sites have since closed. One-year estimates of the global death toll from the loss of USAID stand at around 781,000, and long-term projections are in the range of 14 million. Beyond the staggering human toll, there’s bound to be a less obvious domestic cost from the justified erosion of goodwill and diplomacy wrought by this administration’s callous actions. Stateside, the Trump White House has also taken an axe to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), arguing that disaster relief should be shifted to individual states. Never mind the obvious risk of exhausting state budgets, creating uneven recovery patterns, and losing large-scale coordination for major crises—the prospect of weaning disaster-stricken Americans off the government teat was simply too attractive! Through staffing reductions that reduced FEMA’s workforce by 17% last year, terminated grants that left billions in funding up in the air, and the addition of administrative hurdles, FEMA is now much weaker than it was before inauguration. That weakness has thankfully only reared its head in relatively mild ways thus far. No domestic disaster in Trump 2 has yet been substantially exacerbated by FEMA Lite. A lot of disaster fund requests in that time have been delayed or denied, however, and a disproportionate amount of them have been in Democrat-led states. Meanwhile, slashing roughly 28% of the Treasury Department’s workforce has degraded taxpayer services; hollowing out the CFPB has cost Americans $15 billion in overdraft and credit card late fees alone; and gutting the Office for Civil Rights within the Department of Education has slowed or recklessly dismissed thousands of discrimination cases. Little by little, the value of having high-functioning federal infrastructure is starting to become harder for anyone not in deep denial to dismiss or ignore. The toothpaste is out of the tube Perhaps the worst part about Trump and his enablers diving whole-hog into dismantling the administrative state is that it won’t be rebuilt any time soon, if ever. It’s a whole lot easier to swing a wrecking ball, after all, than it is to mount an ambitious construction project (unless it’s a ballroom-size monument to the president’s ego). When experienced staff leave specialized jobs, they often leave a crucial knowledge gap in their wake. When working relationships with outside agencies and other countries are severed, it takes a lot of time and effort to forge new ones—especially if those previous partners now consider your team unreliable. And when research and data collection projects come to a stop because of lost grant money, they seldom start back up again. Many of the problems Americans now face because of our weakened institutions, and the ones we may face in the near future, cannot be resolved with the stroke of a pen from an incoming majority-Democrat government. For instance, Kennedy could be impeached on January 4 and billions in public-health grants restored the day after, and the U.S. would still be far away from where we stood in January 2025. An epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins University recently estimated it will take at least five years to reclaim measles elimination status in the U.S. Getting rid of measles required decades of unflashy work involving vaccination campaigns and other public-health initiatives. Getting rid of our elimination status took less than two years.If we ever want to get it back, not only will we have to play the Uno Reverse Card on much of what’s happened during Trump 2, but we’ll also have to collectively let go of the myth that strong federal institutions are somehow the biggest problem in America, rather than a source of solutions.

Recent findings suggest that although Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a waiver for lifesaving humanitarian assistance programs, he added a laundry list of politically charged exemptions. These included programs involving abortions, family planning, “gender or DEI ideology programs,” and transgender surgeries. Because HIV/AIDS prevention didn’t fall under that waiver, and thanks to severe cuts to the George W. Bush-created President’s Emergency Strategy for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), 1,700 HIV treatment sites have since closed. One-year estimates of the global death toll from the loss of USAID stand at around 781,000, and long-term projections are in the range of 14 million.

Beyond the staggering human toll, there’s bound to be a less obvious domestic cost from the justified erosion of goodwill and diplomacy wrought by this administration’s callous actions.

Recent findings suggest that stateside, the Trump White House has also taken an axe to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), arguing that disaster relief should be shifted to individual states. Never mind the obvious risk of exhausting state budgets, creating uneven recovery patterns, and losing large-scale coordination for major crises—the prospect of weaning disaster-stricken Americans off the government teat was simply too attractive!

In a recent development, through staffing reductions that reduced FEMA’s workforce by 17% last year, terminated grants that left billions in funding up in the air, and the addition of administrative hurdles, FEMA is now much weaker than it was before inauguration. That weakness has thankfully only reared its head in relatively mild ways thus far. No domestic disaster in Trump 2 has yet been substantially exacerbated by FEMA Lite. A lot of disaster fund requests in that time have been delayed or denied, however, and a disproportionate amount of them have been in Democrat-led states.

Meanwhile, slashing roughly 28% of the Treasury Department’s workforce has degraded taxpayer services; hollowing out the CFPB has cost Americans $15 billion in overdraft and credit card late fees alone; and gutting the Office for Civil Rights within the Department of Education has slowed or recklessly dismissed thousands of discrimination cases.

Little by little, the value of having high-functioning federal infrastructure is starting to become harder for anyone not in deep denial to dismiss or ignore.

According to recent reports, perhaps the worst part about Trump and his enablers diving whole-hog into dismantling the administrative state is that it won’t be rebuilt any time soon, if ever. It’s a whole lot easier to swing a wrecking ball, after all, than it is to mount an ambitious construction project (unless it’s a ballroom-size monument to the president’s ego).

When experienced staff leave specialized jobs, they often leave a crucial knowledge gap in their wake. When working relationships with outside agencies and other countries are severed, it takes a lot of time and effort to forge new ones—especially if those previous partners now consider your team unreliable. And when research and data collection projects come to a stop because of lost grant money, they seldom start back up again.

Many of the problems Americans now face because of our weakened institutions, and the ones we may face in the near future, cannot be resolved with the stroke of a pen from an incoming majority-Democrat government. For instance, Kennedy could be impeached on January 4 and billions in public-health grants restored the day after, and the U.S. would still be far away from where we stood in January 2025. An epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins University recently estimated it will take at least five years to reclaim measles elimination status in the U.S.

Getting rid of measles required decades of unflashy work involving vaccination campaigns and other public-health initiatives. Getting rid of our elimination status took less than two years.If we ever want to get it back, not only will we have to play the Uno Reverse Card on much of what’s happened during Trump 2, but we’ll also have to collectively let go of the myth that strong federal institutions are somehow the biggest problem in America, rather than a source of solutions.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World of Warcraft: Forever's player vs.
  • Recent findings suggest that world of Warcraft: Forever's player vs.
  • While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever's player vs. player systems will work much differently than in previous versions of old-school WoW, developer Blizzard has revealed. While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch. Now, Blizzard has shared more information about how players will earn PvP ranks and honor, with the main takeaway being that players won't have to commit to months of grinding or competing with players on their own faction for top ranks. Honor, a currency earned from killing enemy players and completing battlegrounds and PvP activities, will now exclusively be used to purchase PvP gear and doesn't impact progress towards ranks. Instead, players will rank points by completing daily and weekly PvP quests, fighting in open-world PvP activities like the Gurabashi Arena, and competing in the weekly battleground. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VDNmrrB2k2w In a video detailing the new system, Blizzard mentioned the rank climb will now feel "more varied and predictable" than in the past, when players needed to farm varying amounts of Honor to rank up based on how other players on their same faction were performing. It will also encourage players to engage in different PvP activities each week, instead of simply doing the most efficient one in terms of Honor gained. Though it isn't central to ranking up, Honor still remains as a currency and is used to purchase  PvP gear. Players can start purchasing PvP gear at lower ranks, and then use Honor to upgrade those items into epics once they've reached higher ranks. At the max rank of 14, players unlock access to epic weapons equal in power to gear from the MMO's endgame raids. Blizzard said the biggest way to progress the ranks is by completing weekly season journey quests. For those who might be unable to play for a few weeks and worry about falling behind, each weekly quest doesn't disappear and can be completed later in the season. Forever's PvP rank grind will still take several months of dedicated play (according to Blizzard, players can expect to hit max rank by week eight or nine of a season), but the amount of actual time required will be far less. That's thanks to players on the same faction no longer competing to farm the most Honor in order to achieve top ranks, something that resulted in players of original WoW and WoW Classic grinding battlegrounds for 12 or more hours a day for months on end. "WoW: Forever's Honor system keeps you coming back each week, rather than grinding every day," Blizzard said. "We hope this is a more approachable system that still provides a healthy challenge as you climb to max rank." This isn't the first time Blizzard has revamped classic WoW's Honor system. Though it kept the infamous old system in place for WoW Classic's launch in 2019, it finally made changes in 2023. It kept the Honor grind somewhat intact, but removed the competition between players on the same faction, instead requiring players meet certain Honor thresholds each week to rank up. Forever looks to be a hit for Blizzard so far, with more than 15 million characters created and a record breaking number of concurrent, returning, and weekly players. Despite the game's massive launch and a banner year for WoW in general, it wasn't enough to snag the MMO a nomination for Best Ongoing Game at The Game Awards. In other Forever news, Blizzard recently hotfixed a major dungeon exploit that saw some players, including prominent streamers, earn thousands of gold, only for Blizzard to then remove the ill-gotten gains and issue temporary account suspensions to the worst offenders.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, for years, I thought I knew what separated my moving firm from others.
  • In a recent development, and I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, for years, I thought I knew what separated my moving firm from others. I’m a fourth-generation mover and have worked in this industry professionally since I was 18. My father always said moving was in my blood — hence our name, Can’t Quit Moving. I built my business on lessons passed down through my family: Work hard, treat people and their belongings with respect and do the job the right way. After hearing countless moving horror stories from customers, I knew we operated differently.

In a recent development, and I thought that was enough: doing honest work and making sure people had a good moving experience. I certainly didn’t see our everyday work as content, as something other people would want to know more about or as something that could help grow the company. That changed when someone from outside the industry spent a day with us.

During the pandemic, a good friend of mine who worked as a cameraman was out of work, so he joined our crew for a day. At the end of it, he climbed into the truck looking rattled. “That was a crazy day,” he told me. My response: “That was a Tuesday.”.

According to recent reports, every day, we dealt with closing delays, low bridges, furniture that wouldn’t fit, last-minute additions and customers navigating one of the most stressful days of their lives. To me, that was second nature. To him, it was a story, and he told me we needed to film it.

That eventually became an unscripted docuseries about our company, but it also changed how I thought about growing a business. Until then, we had relied solely on word of mouth. What I hadn’t realized was that showing people what sets us apart from the competition could become a growth strategy.

When you spend every day doing the same thing, you lose sight of what makes it interesting. I didn’t think twice about the problems we encountered on a move, because solving them was my job. But to an outsider, the process was wild. Parking and loading our truck, for example, fascinated our cameraman. It made me realize that the work my team and I do takes real skill.

That’s something business owners in any industry can overlook. You don’t need a glamorous product or a business built for social media to have a story worth telling. A contractor solving a job site matter, a restaurant prepping for a Saturday night or a bookseller opening their store all have something customers rarely get to see.

According to recent reports, simply put, your best content could already be happening. You just have to recognize and document it.

It has been revealed that when we started filming, I had to unlearn some of my business owner instincts. After our second day, my wife paused a piece of footage and asked what I had been thinking in that moment. The truth was, I had been thinking plenty. I just wasn’t saying it.

I was trained to stay calm even when things went off the rails. My wife told me to talk to the camera like I was talking to my best friend. I had to rewire my thinking: Explain the problem. Share what you’re thinking. Admit when you’re frustrated. Just be real.

That taught me the difference between advertising and real storytelling. Business owners spend a lot of time telling customers who they are: We’re trustworthy. We care. We go above and beyond. And so on.

Industry observers note that documenting our work allowed us to show those things instead. Our motto is “We take the stress out of your move,” and now people could see that firsthand: how our crew wraps belongings to protect them from torrential rain, how we responded when a move didn’t go as planned because of an insurance headache and how we treated customers even when we were close to pulling our hair out under high-pressure deadlines. The messy moments showed more about the company than the camera-ready ones.

It has been revealed that other entrepreneurs can learn from this. What do you claim about your business that you could demonstrate instead?

After we finished filming the show, a former customer who worked in the film industry encouraged us to start sharing our story on social media. Creating content consistently has sometimes felt like starting another business, but it also changed how I think about marketing. Traditional advertising usually tries to reach someone around the time they’re ready to buy. Telling a story and building an audience can create a relationship long before that.

Recent findings suggest that that’s especially vital in a business like moving. People don’t need movers every month. Someone might discover one of our videos today and not move for another year. But if they keep following the firm and seeing our crew at work, we don’t have to introduce ourselves when they’re finally ready for a quote. The audience comes first. The customer can come later.

And we’re starting to see that play out. When we ask newly introduced customers how they found us, more and more of them mention our videos. One man contacted us about moving his lemon trees because he’d seen us move palm trees on Instagram. During another move, a customer’s 6-year-old recognized us from our YouTube Shorts. To me, that was proof: People weren’t just remembering our moving organization. They were remembering us. They felt like they’d gotten to know the people behind the business, and more importantly, they already trusted us.

Don’t get me wrong: You don’t need to create a docuseries to apply this strategy. I’d start with three questions:.

In a recent development, the goal isn’t to capture someone’s attention for the sole purpose of selling something. That’s empty, and it doesn’t build trust. The point is to give viewers, your potential customers, a reason to keep paying attention.

Your competitors can offer similar services. They can lower their prices and make the same claims about why they’re better. What they can’t replicate is your people, your experiences, your perspective and how you do your work.
