#7. How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1748 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Sources indicate that like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires. Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied. Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen. GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY The most important thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money, something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the company went public in 2004. “Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.” Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment nearly 10 years later. “We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.” Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public. “If a company’s employees are coming to work just to make money, it’s over,” venture capitalist Paul Koontz stated in 2004. “There need to be some bigger ambitions, some more fundamental calling that motivates a company.” GIVE WOULD-BE ENTREPRENEURS FREEDOM TO EXPERIMENT One of the biggest risks for post-IPO companies is that their most talented and entrepreneurial employees now have the resources to launch their own ventures. In fact, the effect is so powerful that at least one study has identified a causal link between the rate of IPOs in the economy and the rate of newly introduced firm creation. While it may be impossible to prevent these exits altogether, post-IPO companies should ensure that their most talented staff have the freedom and resources to pursue their own ideas. “There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm said in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the company.” Management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe rolled out a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required. “When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Mark Randall, formerly Adobe’s chief strategist and VP of creativity, told Fast Company. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.” DON’T LET WEALTH CREATE A NEW OFFICE HIERARCHY IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the company. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their network, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job. Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Steven Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture. “The biggest mistake a company can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he said. Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.” PAY ATTENTION TO WELL-BEING AND WORKING CONDITIONS Employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away. And new stressors will also emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. Indeed, one study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined by 10% and 6.6% following IPOs. Post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions. Management may also simply need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In one study, published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996. They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees. “Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.

Sources indicate that like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may no longer need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied.

Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen.

The most crucial thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money, something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the firm went public in 2004.

“Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.”.

Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment nearly 10 years later.

“We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.”.

Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a organization goes public.

In a recent development, “If a company’s employees are coming to work just to make money, it’s over,” venture capitalist Paul Koontz remarked in 2004. “There need to be some bigger ambitions, some more fundamental calling that motivates a company.”.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest risks for post-IPO companies is that their most talented and entrepreneurial employees now have the resources to launch their own ventures. In fact, the effect is so powerful that at least one study has identified a causal link between the rate of IPOs in the economy and the rate of upcoming firm creation.

While it may be impossible to prevent these exits altogether, post-IPO companies should ensure that their most talented staff have the freedom and resources to pursue their own ideas.

“There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm said in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the firm.”.

It has been revealed that management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe launched a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required.

Sources indicate that “When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Mark Randall, formerly Adobe’s chief strategist and VP of creativity, told Fast Manufacturer. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.”.

IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the company. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their network, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job.

Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Steven Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture.

“The biggest mistake a firm can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he remarked.

Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.”.

Sources indicate that employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away.

And new stressors will also emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. Indeed, one study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined by 10% and 6.6% following IPOs.

Post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions.

Recent findings suggest that management may also simply need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In one study, published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996.

They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees.

“Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

According to recent reports, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Valve revealed some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

According to recent reports, the good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company notes it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.

Sources indicate that the bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The manufacturer is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The firm anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

Industry observers note that after delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve introduced the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

It has been revealed that U.K.-based fintech Payhawk declared a $280 million Series C funding round Wednesday, led by Goldman Sachs’ growth equity arm, making it one of Europe’s largest Series C rounds this year, as noted by Sifted. The round values the manufacturer at $2 billion, bringing its total funding to more than $500 million to date.

Founded in 2018, Payhawk is an enterprise financial management platform that helps companies track and manage expenses and procurement using AI agents. Speaking to FinTech magazine, Payhawk’s co-founder and CEO, Hristo Borisov, said the tech giant saw “an incredible growth opportunity and room to bring finance teams AI-native products that combine agents, payment infrastructure, and enterprise controls.”.

According to recent reports, payhawk competes with spend management companies Pleo, Moss, and Spendesk, and states it operates in 33 countries. Notably, the firm remarked it still has 70% of the $100 million it raised in 2022, a round that valued the company at $1 billion. This fresh capital will support its global expansion. Other investors in the round include Greenoaks, Lightspeed, and QED.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
  • The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.
  • Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous firm to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.

The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.

Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous firm to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.

Sources indicate that retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.

The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Massive Tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.

Industry observers note that “We take care of everything,” Han stated. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”.

Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song noted, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.

Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.

It has been revealed that because Everful sources from Chinese factories, ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions and tariffs bear directly on its business. Song said the co-founders have been thinking about geopolitical concerns since day one of building the company, and that this has shaped Everful’s strategy from the outset, leveraging her experience at Alibaba and Bessemer Venture Partners.

It has been revealed that she mentioned the Trump administration’s suspension of the de minimis exemption, which had allowed eligible shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the U.S. duty-free, as one example of a shift in trade policy.

Song explained such changes could favor a model that combines overseas sourcing with local retail sales. “We’re empowering local retailers and brands,” she noted. “Long-term cross-border commerce will be cross-border B2B sourcing plus local selling.”.

Everful looks to use the Series A round to expand its presence in the U.S. and Europe, particularly the U.K., France, and Italy, while investing in AI to automate product customization and other sourcing workflows. It also aims to deepen integrations with e-commerce platforms, building on its Shopify integration as it works toward becoming an end-to-end infrastructure platform for global sourcing.

Sources indicate that the startup employs about 70 full-time staff globally, including 45 in research and development. It has also established an AI operations team to connect engineering and business functions.
